title: Ultra-processed food consumption and diet quality among adolescents in urban Ethiopia: baseline findings from a school-based study
text:
Question 1: Reference
Belete, Kefyalew Taye, et al. ‘Ultra-Processed Food Consumption and Diet Quality among Adolescents in Urban Ethiopia: Baseline Findings from a School-Based Study’. Scientific Reports, Sept. 2026. www.nature.com, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-68004-9.


Question 2: Research question
The research aimed to find how much ultra-processed foods such as snacks, sweetened drinks, etc. make up of the diets of teenagers in Adama city, Ethiopia. It’s important because the researchers talked about how little information on this topic is available for low and middle-income countries like in sub-Saharan Africa. They also talked about the overlooked consequences that come with an ultra processes, food, rich diet, such as obesity and diabetes.


Question 3: Data
The research focussed on 713 high school students in Adama City and was collected between October and November of 2024. The data was collected by surveying 29 private schools and 15 public schools.


Question 4: Results

around 92% of high school students consume at least one ultra processed food a week
students from middle income and higher families, showed a smaller consumption of UPFs
out of all the grades that were surveyed, grade 12 students seem to be consuming the most



Question 5: Cited articles

Story, Mary, et al. ‘Individual and Environmental Influences on Adolescent Eating Behaviors’. Journal of the American Dietetic Association, vol. 102, no. 3, Mar. 2002, pp. S40–51. DOI.org (Crossref), https://doi.org/10.1016/S0002-8223(02)90421-9.

Question 6: Questions for the authors

did the students from middle class families consume less UPFs because they could afford healthier ones or there were more educated on them than lower income students?
was their significant difference with European high schoolstudents?
how does climate impact ones UPF consumption?

@article{li_action_2026,
    title = {Action chunking transformer-based imitation learning with dynamic programming optimization for low-cost robotic assembly tasks},
    copyright = {2026 The Author(s)},

    url = {https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-63709-3},
    doi = {10.1038/s41598-026-63709-3},
    abstract = {Nowadays, many studies focus on using AI tools to improve the performance of manipulators in fields such as assembly. One popular approach is the Action Chunking Transformer (ACT), which enables robots to execute assembly tasks more efficiently. However, this method still faces challenges in achieving reliable assembly performance, particularly for low-cost manipulators with limited mechanical repeatability. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel Dynamic Programming–based Action Chunking Transformer (DP-ACT) framework. By integrating dynamic programming into the ACT inference chain, the method provides local trajectory correction while maintaining the implemented control-loop frequency. The proposed framework was implemented on a low-cost SO100 robotic manipulator equipped with Feetech actuators and evaluated through a three-stage precision-oriented assembly task. A total of 160 teleoperated demonstrations were collected for offline training, and 100 assembly trials were conducted for evaluation. Experimental results indicate that DP-ACT increases the assembly success rate from 62\% to 82\% and significantly improves trajectory efficiency while maintaining comparable task completion times.},

title: Potential of artificial intelligence in reducing energy and carbon emissions of commercial buildings at scale
text:
Reference
@article{ding2024potential,
  title={Potential of Artificial Intelligence in Reducing Energy and Carbon Emissions of Commercial Buildings at Scale},
  author={Ding, Chao and Ke, Jing and Levine, Mark and Granderson, Jessica and Zhou, Nan},
  journal={Nature Communications},
  volume={15},
  number={1},
  pages={5916},
  year={2024},
  doi={10.1038/s41467-024-50088-4}
}


What, why, objective?
Artificial intelligence has emerged as a technology to enhance productivity and improve life quality. However, its role in building energy efficiency and carbon emission reduction has not been systematically studied. This study evaluated artificial intelligence’s potential in the building sector, focusing on medium office buildings in the United States.


How is the problem solved?
A methodology was developed to assess and quantify potential emissions reductions. Key areas identified were equipment, occupancy influence, control and operation, and design and construction. Six scenarios were used to estimate energy and emissions savings across representative climate zones.


Result
Here we show that artificial intelligence could reduce cost premiums, enhancing high energy efficiency and net zero building penetration. Adopting artificial intelligence could reduce energy consumption and carbon emissions by approximately 8% to 19% in 2050.


Impact
Combining with energy policy and low-carbon power generation could approximately reduce energy consumption by 40% and carbon emissions by 90% compared to business-as-usual scenarios in 2050.

82%, 64%

title: Habitual video gaming predicts multitasking performance while the role of cognitive capacity remains inconclusive
text:
Question 1: Reference

@article{hilla2025gaming,
  author  = {Hilla, Yannik and Stasch, Sophie-Marie and Mack, Wolfgang},
  title   = {Habitual video gaming predicts multitasking performance while the role of cognitive capacity remains inconclusive},
  journal = {Scientific Reports},
  year    = {2025},
  volume  = {15},
  pages   = {37362},
  doi     = {10.1038/s41598-025-25260-5},
  url     = {https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-25260-5}
}


Question 2: Research question
Does greater video-gaming experience predict better multitasking performance, and is this relationship explained by greater cognitive capacity?
Video gaming has been associated with better attention and information processing, but it is still unclear why gamers may perform better on complex multitasking tasks. The study tries to understand the mechanism behind this relationship.


Question 3: Data

Who / Cases: 59 participants were analyzed, aged 18–29 years with an average age of about 23. There were 45 men and 14 women, and most were military officer cadets.
What / Variables:

Video-gaming experience: weekly gaming time, previous gaming experience, and self-rated gaming expertise.
Multitasking performance: performance on system monitoring, tracking, communication, and resource-management tasks.
Cognitive capacity: information-processing speed and short-term/working-memory capacity.
Other variables included age, gender, military experience, media multitasking, and flight experience.

When: Data were collected from October to December 2023.
Where: The testing was conducted in a university laboratory, primarily associated with Universität der Bundeswehr München in Germany.
How was the data collected? Participants completed:

A visual short-term-memory test.
The openMATB multitasking test.
Questionnaires about demographics, media multitasking, and video-gaming experience.

Gaming experience was mostly self-reported, while cognitive capacity and multitasking performance were measured experimentally using computer tasks.



Question 4: Results

Main results:

Greater video-gaming experience was associated with better multitasking performance.
Cognitive capacity did not significantly explain the relationship between gaming and multitasking.

Conclusion: Gaming experience may predict better multitasking performance, but the study could not clearly determine why this relationship exists.
Do the data support the conclusions? The data support the finding that gaming experience predicts better multitasking performance. However, they did not support the hypothesis that cognitive capacity explains this relationship. The relatively small sample size is also a limitation.

title: Aleksandre - Perceived humanness and empathy are dissociated in relationship advice generated by a large language model
text:
Question 1: Reference
@article{kleinberg_perceived_2026,
    title = {Perceived humanness and empathy are dissociated in relationship advice generated by a large language model},
    issn = {2041-1723},
    url = {https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-77350-1},
    doi = {10.1038/s41467-026-77350-1},
    language = {en},
    urldate = {2026-09-08},
    journal = {Nature Communications},
    author = {Kleinberg, Bennett and Zegers, Jari and Festor, Jonas and Vida, Stefana and Präsent, Julian and Loconte, Riccardo and Peereboom, Sanne},
    month = sep,
    year = {2026},
}


Question 2: Research question
The research question is whether perceived humanness and empathy are dissociated in relationship advice generated by a large language model, and how incentives to convey humanness and task characteristics shape perceptions of textual content.
It matters because differentiating generated and human-written content is becoming increasingly difficult, and the research showed that perceived humanness depends on incentives to appear human and the context in which writing is produced.


Question 3: Data
The article states that 5 studies were conducted. In study 1, 587 participants were recruited via Prolific. They were randomly assigned to the adversarial group (n=315) or the naive condition group (n=272), 57 participants failed the manipulation check and were excluded.
All participants performed a writing task. Different details about fictious relationships were given in the task, resulting in 8 stimulus sets. Participants wrote relationship advice (min. 500 characters). Same task was done by GPT-4 which was prompted with identical questions as the humans.


Question 4: Results
The study conducted that LLMs reportedly generate text indistinguishable from humans. Another finding was that LLMs, but not humans, adjusted their writing noticeably when instructed to be particularly human.
The data from the studies supports the findings. Study 1 summary stated “when instructed to be as human as possible, the LLM could drastically increase the humanness perception (+39.3%) while humans could not (+2.6%).
